source.title: Exploring Scaling Trends in LLM Robustness
source.citation: Nikolaus H. R. Howe et al., 2024
source.authors: Nikolaus H. R. Howe; Michal Zajac; Ian R. McKenzie; O. Hollinsworth; Tom Tseng; Pierre-Luc Bacon; Adam Gleave

record.tranche_reason: The study measures clean downstream-task accuracy across model sizes, which bears on V6, but it does not measure held-out pretraining loss or test the original loss-scaling recipe.
record.gate_note: The paper studies adversarial robustness, not held-out cross-entropy scaling. Its attack-success and adversarial-training results do not measure any listed version. The clean-data accuracy results in Table 1 are included because they directly compare downstream task performance across model sizes (V6).
record.test_reason: The study is about adversarial robustness. Its only overlap with the claim is clean accuracy of finetuned classifiers (Table 1, Fig. 8, Fig. 9). That accuracy is a pre-attack capability check, used to filter which examples are scored for attack success. It is not a test of whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or with pretraining loss. Table 1 gives only the smallest and largest model per family, several tasks sit at ceiling (0.98–0.995), and no loss or scaling fit is reported. Kaplan et al. is used only for the 6ND FLOP approximation (App. E) and cited in related work. So no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Absent safety training, model size alone does not reliably improve robustness. Attack and defense compute each scale smoothly. Attackers outpace defenders at fixed model size, but larger adversarially trained models may favour defense long-run. No claims about loss scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines adversarial robustness and clean downstream accuracy rather than fitting held-out language-model loss scaling laws or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Task and model family: clean accuracy changes with size on some reported tasks and stays the same on others; the generative StrongREJECT results differ from the classification results.

fits_no_version.finding: Without safety training, larger Pythia and Qwen2.5 classifiers are not consistently more robust to GCG, BEAST or RandomToken attacks. The trend is noisy and task-dependent (Fig. 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial robustness of LM classifiers does not reliably improve with parameter count absent safety training.

fits_no_version.finding: Attack success rate rises smoothly with attack compute and is roughly linear in logit vs log-compute. This implies a power law at low success rates (Fig. 3, App. C.5.1). Adversarial training compute reduces attack success smoothly; larger models are more sample-efficient but less compute-efficient (Fig. 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attack and defense success scale smoothly (power-law-like) with attack and adversarial-training compute.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: For the clean accuracy results relevant to V6, Table 1 reports only the smallest and largest models, not the full size sweep; uncertainty estimates are not given there. The study does not report held-out pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: Attack-success and adversarial-training scaling results were not included because they measure robustness rather than any listed claim version. No Table 1 values were omitted.

untested.parts: No power-law fits of loss in other modalities or regimes. Finetuning is used, but its loss is not fitted against scale.
No relation of downstream accuracy to scale or loss is fitted. Clean accuracy appears only as a capability check.
No exponent fitting or comparison of fits.

missing.what: Full-sweep clean accuracy across all Pythia and Qwen2.5 sizes, if anyone later treats finetuned accuracy as V6 evidence. Text: all models >85% except Helpful/Harmless, none reach 75% there.
missing.locator: Appendix C.1, Figure 8; Figure 9 for StrongREJECT

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the Table 1 rows to V6 and gave supports, limits_scope and challenges labels. These are removed. The values are pre-attack capability checks used to select evaluable examples, reported only at size endpoints, often at ceiling (0.995). StrongREJECT values reflect safety post-training. They cannot show downstream predictability with scale or loss. The only link to the original sources is use of Kaplan's 6ND compute approximation.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run held-out loss from smaller runs.
Compute-optimal allocation between parameters and tokens.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Scaling-law form in other modalities or training regimes.
No pretraining-loss-to-downstream-performance relation is tested; only selected clean-task accuracies at the smallest and largest models are reported.
Dependence of held-out-loss exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup or fitting choices.

reader_labels.condition: Qwen2.5 Instruct, StrongREJECT, smallest versus largest model
reader_labels.reason: Clean-data accuracy rises from 0.556 to 0.981 as size increases, in rows r21–r22; the paper also states that larger models significantly outperform smaller ones on the generative task.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Finetuned classification tasks with reported size endpoints
reader_labels.reason: Accuracy increases on some tasks but is unchanged on others, and the authors characterize large and small classification-model accuracies as similar (rows r1–r20).
